lesson.subject: evidence
lesson.topic: Hearsay: definition and statements that are not hearsay
lesson.title: What Counts as Hearsay? (FRE 801)
lesson.author: Chandler Burleson (draft assisted)

items.title: What is a "statement"?
items.rule: A statement is a person's oral assertion, written assertion, or nonverbal conduct, if the person intended the conduct as an assertion. The declarant is the person who made the statement.
items.tip: No intent to assert, no statement, so no hearsay. Only people make statements.
items.hook: Say it, write it, or point it. A nod counts, a sneeze does not.

items.title: The hearsay test
items.rule: Hearsay is a statement that (1) the declarant does not make while testifying at the current trial or hearing, and (2) a party offers in evidence to prove the truth of the matter asserted in it. Hearsay is not admissible unless a federal statute, the FRE, or other Supreme Court rules provide otherwise.
items.tip: Ask two things: was it said outside this trial, and do we need it to be true?
items.hook: Out of court + offered for truth = hearsay. OC + TOMA.

items.title: Not offered for its truth
items.rule: A statement offered for any purpose other than proving the truth of what it asserts is not hearsay. Common examples: effect on the listener (notice, fear, reasonableness), legally operative words (verbal acts like an offer or a threat), and impeachment with an inconsistent statement.
items.tip: If the words matter just because they were said, it's not hearsay.
items.hook: Heard it, did it, or contradicted it: the words work without being true.
items.reviewer_notes: Categories come from case law applying 801(c)(2), not the rule text itself.

items.title: Prior statements of a testifying witness
items.rule: Not hearsay if the declarant testifies, is subject to cross-examination about the prior statement, and the statement: (A) is inconsistent with the testimony and was given under penalty of perjury at a trial, hearing, other proceeding, or deposition; (B) is consistent with the testimony and is offered to rebut a charge of recent fabrication or improper influence or motive, or to rehabilitate credibility attacked on another ground; or (C) identifies a person as someone the declarant perceived earlier.
items.tip: The witness must be on the stand and cross-examinable; then sworn inconsistencies, rehab consistencies, and IDs come in.

items.title: Opposing party's statement
items.rule: Not hearsay if offered against a party and the statement was: (A) made by the party in an individual or representative capacity; (B) adopted or believed true by the party; (C) made by a person the party authorized to speak on the subject; (D) made by the party's agent or employee on a matter within the scope of that relationship while it existed; or (E) made by the party's coconspirator during and in furtherance of the conspiracy. The statement must be considered but does not by itself establish authority, the relationship, or the conspiracy.
items.tip: Anything your opponent (or their people) said can be used against them; it need not have been against interest when said.
items.hook: "Own it, adopt it, authorize it, employ it, conspire it."

items.prompt: Nonverbal conduct is a statement only if the person ___ it as an assertion.
items.explanation: FRE 801(a): conduct counts only when intended as an assertion.

items.prompt: Hearsay is a statement the declarant does not make while testifying at the ___ trial or hearing, offered to prove the ___ of the matter asserted.
A testifying witness's prior inconsistent statement is not hearsay if it was given under penalty of ___ at a trial, hearing, other proceeding, or ___.
A statement by a party's employee is not hearsay if it concerns a matter within the ___ of that relationship and was made while it ___.
items.explanation: FRE 801(d)(2)(D). Speaking authority is not required, unlike (C).

items.prompt: A coconspirator's statement is not hearsay if made during and in ___ of the conspiracy.

items.stem: In a suit over a collision at an intersection, the plaintiff calls Maya, who testifies that just after the crash a jogger she did not know yelled, "The pickup blew straight through the red!" The plaintiff offers this to prove the pickup ran the red light. The defendant objects.
items.question: Under the hearsay definition, how should the court classify Maya's testimony about the jogger's words?

options.text: Not hearsay, because Maya is testifying in court and can be cross-examined.
options.why_wrong: The declarant is the jogger, not Maya. Maya's presence does not cure it.

options.text: Hearsay, because it is the jogger's out-of-court assertion offered to prove that the pickup ran the red light.
Not hearsay, because the jogger is unidentified.
options.why_wrong: Anonymity does not change the definition; it may affect exceptions.

options.text: Not hearsay, because it describes an event the jogger perceived.
options.why_wrong: Perception goes to some exceptions, not to the definition.

items.explanation: FRE 801(c): out-of-court statement offered for its truth. It is hearsay by definition; whether an exception such as FRE 803(1) or (2) admits it is a separate step.

items.stem: A shopper slipped on spilled detergent in a grocery store and sued for negligence. To show the store knew of the hazard, the shopper offers testimony from a cashier that, 20 minutes before the fall, a customer told the store manager, "There's soap all over aisle 7."
items.question: Is the cashier's testimony about the customer's remark hearsay?

options.text: Yes, because the customer is not testifying.
options.why_wrong: Out of court alone is not enough; purpose matters.

options.text: Yes, unless the customer is shown to be unavailable.
options.why_wrong: Unavailability matters only for FRE 804 exceptions.

options.text: No, because it is offered to show the manager had notice, not that soap was actually on the floor.
No, because it is a statement of a party opponent.
options.why_wrong: The customer is not the store, its agent, or its employee.

items.explanation: FRE 801(c)(2): offered for its effect on the listener (notice), not its truth. A limiting instruction may be requested under FRE 105.

items.stem: After an elderly man died, his nephew and his estate dispute who owns his antique pocket watch. The nephew offers testimony from a neighbor who saw the uncle hand him the watch and say, "This is yours now. I want you to have it."
items.question: Is the neighbor's testimony about the uncle's words hearsay?

options.text: Yes, because the uncle is dead and cannot be cross-examined.
options.why_wrong: Unavailability does not affect whether a statement is hearsay.

options.text: No, because the words are legally operative; they help make the gift itself.
Yes, because it is offered to prove the nephew owns the watch.
options.why_wrong: The words create the gift; they are not reporting a fact.

options.text: No, because the neighbor personally saw the uncle hand over the watch.
options.why_wrong: The neighbor's perception doesn't change what the uncle's words are used for; the reason is their legal effect.

items.explanation: FRE 801(c)(2): verbal acts (words of gift, offer, acceptance) are not offered for truth of an assertion. They have legal effect simply because they were said.

items.stem: In a fraud prosecution, Lee testified before the grand jury that the defendant told him to backdate invoices. At trial, Lee testifies that the defendant never discussed invoices with him. Earlier, Lee also told an investigator in an unsworn interview that the defendant ordered the backdating. The prosecutor wants the jury to consider Lee's earlier accounts as proof of what happened.
items.question: Which prior statement may the jury consider as substantive evidence?

options.text: Both statements, because Lee is testifying and subject to cross-examination.
options.why_wrong: 801(d)(1)(A) also requires the statement to be under penalty of perjury at a proceeding or deposition.

options.text: Only the grand jury testimony.
Only the investigator interview, because it was made closer in time to the events.
options.why_wrong: Timing is irrelevant; the interview was not sworn in a proceeding.

options.text: Neither; prior inconsistent statements may be used only to impeach.
options.why_wrong: That is the common-law rule; the FRE admit sworn ones substantively.

items.explanation: FRE 801(d)(1)(A): a sworn inconsistent statement at a proceeding (grand jury counts) is not hearsay. The unsworn interview may still be used to impeach (FRE 613).

items.stem: A delivery van owned by FastFreight Co. rear-ended the plaintiff's car. Still at the scene, the van's driver, a FastFreight employee on his route, told the plaintiff, "I'm so sorry, I was checking my phone for the next address." The plaintiff sues only FastFreight and offers the driver's remark. The driver was fired a week later.
items.question: Is the driver's statement admissible against FastFreight over a hearsay objection?

options.text: No, because the driver had no authority to speak for FastFreight.
options.why_wrong: Speaking authority is required for (C), not (D).

options.text: No, because the driver is no longer employed by FastFreight.
options.why_wrong: The relationship need only exist when the statement was made.

options.text: Yes, because it was a statement against the driver's interest.
options.why_wrong: FRE 804(b)(3) requires unavailability; it is not the best answer.

options.text: Yes, because it was made by FastFreight's employee about a matter within the scope of employment while employed.

items.explanation: FRE 801(d)(2)(D): employee's statement on a matter within the scope of the relationship, made while it existed, is not hearsay when offered against the employer.

items.stem: In a theft prosecution, a bartender testifies that the night the tip jar went missing, a regular said to the defendant across the bar, "You're the one who swiped the tip jar." The defendant laughed and replied, "Prove it. Drinks are on me tonight." No police were present.
items.question: How should the court rule on the defendant's hearsay objection to the regular's accusation?

options.text: Overrule it, if the jury could find the defendant manifested that he adopted the accusation as true.
Sustain it, because the regular is not a party.
options.why_wrong: Under (B), a non-party's words become the party's own when adopted.

options.text: Sustain it, because silence or evasion can never be an adoption.
options.why_wrong: Adoption by conduct or a non-denial can qualify where a reasonable person would deny.

options.text: Overrule it, because accusations are never offered for their truth.
options.why_wrong: Here it is offered for truth; that's why an exclusion is needed.

items.explanation: FRE 801(d)(2)(B): a statement the party manifested that it adopted or believed to be true. Whether he adopted it is a preliminary question (FRE 104).
items.reviewer_notes: Chandler: confirm FRE 104(a) vs 104(b) treatment you want to teach for adoption.

items.prompt: A witness pointing to the defendant when asked "Who hit you?" is a statement.
items.explanation: Nonverbal conduct intended as an assertion is a statement. FRE 801(a).

items.prompt: A coconspirator's statement, by itself, can establish that the conspiracy existed.
items.explanation: The statement must be considered but does not by itself establish the conspiracy. FRE 801(d)(2) (final sentence).

items.prompt: A prior statement identifying a person is not hearsay even if the declarant never testifies.
items.explanation: The declarant must testify and be subject to cross about the statement. FRE 801(d)(1).

items.stem: Dana is charged with arson. Her former roommate, Ray, testifies for the government that Dana told him she set the fire. On cross, defense counsel shows that Ray was arrested on drug charges in March and signed a cooperation agreement in April, suggesting he invented the story to get leniency. On redirect, the government offers two earlier statements by Ray, each consistent with his trial testimony: (1) a text Ray sent his sister in February, before his arrest, saying Dana "admitted torching the place"; and (2) a written statement Ray gave agents in May.
items.question: Which of Ray's prior statements is admissible as substantive evidence to rebut the charge of fabrication?

options.text: Both, because Ray testified and is subject to cross-examination.
options.why_wrong: Being cross-examinable is necessary but not sufficient.

options.text: Only the May statement to agents, because it was made to law enforcement.
options.why_wrong: It came after the motive to fabricate arose, so it does not rebut the charge.

options.text: Only the February text to his sister.
Neither, because prior consistent statements are bolstering and inadmissible.
options.why_wrong: 801(d)(1)(B) admits them when they actually rebut the charge.

items.explanation: FRE 801(d)(1)(B)(i) admits a consistent statement offered to rebut a charge of recent fabrication or improper motive. Under Tome v. United States, 513 U.S. 150 (1995), the statement must predate the alleged motive. The February text came before the arrest and deal; the May statement came after.
hints: When did Ray's motive to lie arise?
Map each statement against the March arrest.
items.reviewer_notes: Tome's premotive requirement is case law; confirm whether to teach the 2014 amendment's (B)(ii) rehab path here or in a later lesson.
